meta.title: General timeline of Christian history
meta.dating: Conventional scholarly dates; approx:true marks uncertain dates; ranges and disputes are in English `note` fields and research/history-notes.md. Negative years are BC.

title.es: Primera Carta de Clemente a los Corintios
title.en: First Letter of Clement to the Corinthians (1 Clement)

summary.es: Figura destacada de la Iglesia de Roma a fines del siglo I; las listas antiguas de obispos lo ubican como tercer o cuarto sucesor de Pedro. Su carta a los corintios, escrita en nombre de la Iglesia de Roma para resolver la deposición de unos presbíteros, es uno de los escritos cristianos no canónicos más antiguos que se conservan.
summary.en: A leading figure of the Roman church at the end of the first century; ancient episcopal lists place him third or fourth after Peter. His letter to the Corinthians, written in the name of the Roman church to address the removal of presbyters, is one of the oldest surviving non-canonical Christian writings.

fathers.note: 1 Clement is conventionally dated c. 96 (end of Domitian's reign); a minority of scholars argue for c. 70 or a broader 80–100 range. Death date c. 99–101 is traditional only.

summary.es: Breve manual anónimo de enseñanza moral, bautismo, ayuno, oración y Eucaristía, probablemente compilado en Siria o Palestina. Redescubierto en 1873 en un códice de Constantinopla, es un testimonio temprano de la vida litúrgica y la organización de las primeras comunidades.
summary.en: A short anonymous manual on moral teaching, baptism, fasting, prayer and the Eucharist, probably compiled in Syria or Palestine. Rediscovered in 1873 in a Constantinople codex, it is an early witness to the liturgical life and organization of the first communities.

fathers.note: Kind "work": `died` holds a conventional composition year, not a death. Scholarly dating ranges from c. 50 to c. 120 (often "late first century"); the text is likely composite. Provenance (Syria, Palestine or Egypt) is debated.

title.es: Siete cartas (a los Efesios, Magnesios, Tralianos, Romanos, Filadelfios, Esmirniotas y a Policarpo)
title.en: Seven letters (to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans and to Polycarp)

summary.es: Obispo de Antioquía que, según la tradición, fue llevado preso a Roma y martirizado bajo Trajano. Las siete cartas que escribió durante el viaje insisten en la unidad en torno al obispo, presbíteros y diáconos, y polemizan contra quienes negaban la realidad de la carne de Cristo.
summary.en: Bishop of Antioch who, according to tradition, was taken as a prisoner to Rome and martyred under Trajan. The seven letters he wrote on the journey stress unity around the bishop, presbyters and deacons, and argue against those who denied the reality of Christ's flesh.

fathers.note: Traditional date of martyrdom c. 107–110 (under Trajan, r. 98–117), based on Eusebius. Some scholars (e.g. Barnes, Hübner) argue for a later date, c. 120–140. Authenticity of the seven-letter "middle recension" is the majority view; longer and shorter recensions also exist.

title.es: Exposición de los oráculos del Señor (fragmentos)
title.en: Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord (fragments)

summary.es: Obispo de Hierápolis que, según Ireneo, había escuchado a Juan y fue compañero de Policarpo. Su obra se perdió, pero los fragmentos citados por Ireneo y Eusebio contienen las noticias más antiguas sobre el origen de los evangelios de Marcos y Mateo.
summary.en: Bishop of Hierapolis who, according to Irenaeus, had heard John and was a companion of Polycarp. His work is lost, but fragments quoted by Irenaeus and Eusebius contain the earliest reports on the origins of the Gospels of Mark and Matthew.

fathers.note: Dates of Papias are very uncertain. The Exposition is usually dated c. 110–130, but some scholars (Bartlet, Yarbrough, Bauckham) argue for c. 95–110. Birth c. 60–70 and death c. 130 are estimates.

summary.es: Tratado anónimo, atribuido en la Antigüedad a Bernabé, que lee el Antiguo Testamento de forma tipológica y alegórica en clave cristiana. Fue incluido en el Códice Sinaítico y algunos autores alejandrinos lo citaron como Escritura, aunque no entró en el canon.
summary.en: An anonymous treatise, attributed in antiquity to Barnabas, that reads the Old Testament typologically and allegorically in a Christian key. It was included in Codex Sinaiticus and cited as Scripture by some Alexandrian writers, but did not enter the canon.

fathers.note: Kind "work": `died` = conventional composition year. Written after 70 (refers to the Temple's destruction) and probably before 135; many scholars favor c. 96–100 or c. 130–132. Alexandrian provenance is likely but not certain.

role.es: obra apocalíptica y moral escrita en Roma
role.en: apocalyptic and moral work written in Rome

summary.es: Obra de visiones y exhortaciones morales centrada en la penitencia después del bautismo, escrita en Roma por un tal Hermas. Fue muy leída en la Iglesia antigua; algunos la consideraron Escritura, pero el Fragmento Muratoriano la admite solo para lectura privada.
summary.en: A work of visions and moral exhortations centered on repentance after baptism, written in Rome by one Hermas. It was widely read in the early Church; some treated it as Scripture, but the Muratorian Fragment allows it only for private reading.

fathers.note: Kind "work": `died` = conventional composition year. The Muratorian Fragment says Hermas was brother of Pius, bishop of Rome (c. 140–154); some sections may be earlier (c. 100). Probably composed in stages.

summary.es: Breve apología anónima dirigida a un pagano culto, conocida por su descripción de los cristianos como “el alma del mundo”. Se conservó en un único manuscrito medieval, destruido en 1870, y suele agruparse con los Padres Apostólicos aunque su género es apologético.
summary.en: A short anonymous apology addressed to an educated pagan, known for describing Christians as "the soul of the world". It survived in a single medieval manuscript, destroyed in 1870, and is usually grouped with the Apostolic Fathers although its genre is apologetic.

fathers.note: Kind "work": `died` = conventional composition year. Date and provenance unknown; proposals range from c. 120 to c. 200 (some later). Chapters 11–12 are probably a separate addition. Region is a placeholder (provenance unknown).

summary.es: Obispo de Esmirna que, según Ireneo, había conocido al apóstol Juan, y que recibió una carta de Ignacio de Antioquía. Su martirio, narrado en el Martirio de Policarpo, es el relato de martirio cristiano más antiguo que se conserva fuera del Nuevo Testamento.
summary.en: Bishop of Smyrna who, according to Irenaeus, had known the apostle John, and who received a letter from Ignatius of Antioch. His death, told in the Martyrdom of Polycarp, is the oldest surviving account of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament.

fathers.note: Martyrdom usually dated 155 or 156; Eusebius places it c. 167. Birth c. 69 is derived from his statement of having served Christ 86 years. Some scholars see the Letter to the Philippians as two letters (ch. 13 written c. 110, the rest later).

summary.es: Filósofo nacido en Flavia Neápolis (Samaria) que, tras su conversión, enseñó en Roma y defendió la fe ante emperadores y ante interlocutores judíos. Su Primera Apología contiene la descripción más antigua conocida de una celebración dominical del bautismo y la Eucaristía; murió mártir en Roma.
summary.en: A philosopher born in Flavia Neapolis (Samaria) who, after his conversion, taught in Rome and defended the faith before emperors and Jewish interlocutors. His First Apology contains the oldest known description of a Sunday baptismal and eucharistic celebration; he died a martyr in Rome.

fathers.note: Martyrdom under the prefect Rusticus, c. 162–168 (often given as 165).

summary.es: Obispo de Sardes de tradición cuartodecimana, es decir, que celebraba la Pascua el 14 de nisán. Su homilía Sobre la Pascua, recuperada en papiros del siglo XX, interpreta la Pascua del Éxodo como figura de la pasión de Cristo; también es la fuente más antigua de una lista cristiana de libros del Antiguo Testamento.
summary.en: A bishop of Sardis in the Quartodeciman tradition, which kept Easter on the 14th of Nisan. His homily On the Pascha, recovered from twentieth-century papyrus finds, reads the Exodus Passover as a figure of Christ's passion; he is also the earliest source for a Christian list of Old Testament books.

fathers.note: Death c. 180 (approximate; Eusebius places his Apology under Marcus Aurelius, c. 170).

summary.es: Obispo de Antioquía y apologista, autor de tres libros dirigidos a un pagano llamado Autólico. Es el primer autor conocido que usa el término griego trias (“tríada”) para referirse a Dios, su Palabra y su Sabiduría.
summary.en: Bishop of Antioch and apologist, author of three books addressed to a pagan named Autolycus. He is the first known writer to use the Greek term trias ("triad") for God, his Word and his Wisdom.

fathers.note: Death c. 183–185.

summary.es: Originario de Asia Menor, donde de joven escuchó a Policarpo, fue presbítero y luego obispo de Lyon tras la persecución de 177. Su obra Contra las herejías refuta los sistemas gnósticos apelando a la Escritura, a la regla de fe y a la sucesión de los obispos en las iglesias apostólicas.
summary.en: A native of Asia Minor who heard Polycarp in his youth, he became presbyter and then bishop of Lyon after the persecution of 177. His Against Heresies refutes Gnostic systems by appealing to Scripture, the rule of faith and the succession of bishops in the apostolic churches.

fathers.note: Birth c. 130–140; death c. 200–202 (later tradition of martyrdom is unconfirmed). Against Heresies survives complete only in Latin translation; the Demonstration only in Armenian.

summary.es: Maestro cristiano en Alejandría, probablemente nacido en Atenas, que dialogó extensamente con la filosofía griega. Presentó la fe como la verdadera “gnosis” y dejó la Alejandría hacia 202 durante la persecución de Septimio Severo.
summary.en: A Christian teacher in Alexandria, probably born in Athens, who engaged extensively with Greek philosophy. He presented the faith as the true "gnosis" and left Alexandria around 202 during the persecution under Septimius Severus.

fathers.note: Death c. 211–216. Ancient martyrologies listed him as a saint; he was removed from the Roman Martyrology in the 16th century; venerated in some Eastern traditions.

title.es: Sobre la prescripción de los herejes

summary.es: Primer gran autor cristiano en latín, cuyo vocabulario teológico (por ejemplo trinitas, persona, substantia) influyó en toda la tradición occidental. En su madurez se acercó al montanismo, por lo que no suele ser venerado como santo, aunque se lo cita ampliamente como testigo de la fe de su época.
summary.en: The first major Christian author in Latin, whose theological vocabulary (e.g. trinitas, persona, substantia) shaped the whole Western tradition. Later in life he moved toward Montanism, so he is not usually venerated as a saint, though he is widely cited as a witness to the faith of his time.

fathers.note: Birth c. 155–160; death unknown, after c. 220 (some say c. 240). Jerome's report that he was a presbyter is debated by modern scholars.

title.es: Refutación de todas las herejías (atribución debatida)

summary.es: Presbítero y escritor de Roma que entró en conflicto con los obispos Ceferino y Calixto y encabezó una comunidad rival. Exiliado a Cerdeña en 235 junto con el obispo Ponciano, se reconcilió y ambos murieron allí; es venerado como mártir.
summary.en: A Roman presbyter and writer who clashed with bishops Zephyrinus and Callistus and led a rival community. Exiled to Sardinia in 235 with bishop Pontian, he was reconciled and both died there; he is venerated as a martyr.

fathers.note: Identity and corpus are among the most debated in patristics: the Apostolic Tradition is often seen as a composite text of uncertain origin; some scholars distinguish two or more authors named Hippolytus.

summary.es: Maestro de Alejandría y luego de Cesarea de Palestina, fue el exégeta bíblico más prolífico de la Iglesia antigua y compiló la Hexapla, una edición comparativa del Antiguo Testamento. Murió tras las torturas sufridas en la persecución de Decio; algunas tesis atribuidas a él y a sus seguidores fueron condenadas en el siglo VI.
summary.en: A teacher in Alexandria and later Caesarea in Palestine, he was the most prolific biblical exegete of the early Church and compiled the Hexapla, a comparative edition of the Old Testament. He died after torture suffered in the Decian persecution; some views attributed to him and his followers were condemned in the sixth century.

fathers.note: Death c. 253–254 at Tyre. The extent to which the 553 condemnations targeted Origen himself or later Origenists is debated.

title.es: Sobre la unidad de la Iglesia católica
title.en: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

summary.es: Retórico convertido que llegó a obispo de Cartago, gobernó su iglesia durante las persecuciones de Decio y Valeriano y abordó la readmisión de los “caídos”. Mantuvo una controversia con el obispo Esteban de Roma sobre el rebautismo de los herejes y murió decapitado en 258.
summary.en: A converted rhetorician who became bishop of Carthage, led his church through the Decian and Valerian persecutions and dealt with the readmission of the "lapsed". He disputed with bishop Stephen of Rome over rebaptizing heretics and was beheaded in 258.

fathers.note: Death date secure (14 September 258); birth c. 200–210 estimated. Two versions of On the Unity ch. 4 exist (the so-called "Primacy text"); both may go back to Cyprian.

role.es: presbítero de Roma y obispo rival
role.en: presbyter of Rome and rival bishop

summary.es: Presbítero romano y teólogo de talla, autor del primer gran tratado latino sobre la Trinidad escrito en Roma. En 251 se opuso a la elección de Cornelio y fue consagrado obispo rival, dando origen a una iglesia separada que rechazaba readmitir a los caídos.
summary.en: A Roman presbyter and capable theologian, author of the first major Latin treatise on the Trinity written in Rome. In 251 he opposed the election of Cornelius and was consecrated a rival bishop, starting a separate church that refused to readmit the lapsed.

fathers.note: Death c. 258 is based on a late tradition of martyrdom under Valerian; uncertain. Not usually counted as a "Father" because of the schism; included as a source.

summary.es: Discípulo de Orígenes y obispo de Alejandría desde 247/248, sobrevivió a las persecuciones de Decio y Valeriano. Sus obras se conservan en fragmentos, entre ellos un análisis del estilo del Apocalipsis que lo llevó a dudar de que su autor fuera el mismo del cuarto evangelio.
summary.en: A pupil of Origen and bishop of Alexandria from 247/248, he survived the Decian and Valerian persecutions. His works survive in fragments, including a stylistic analysis of Revelation that led him to doubt it had the same author as the Fourth Gospel.

fathers.note: Death 264 or 265.

summary.es: Obispo y escritor de Licia, crítico de algunas tesis de Orígenes, en especial sobre el cuerpo resucitado. Su obra más conocida, El banquete, imita el diálogo de Platón para elogiar la virginidad; según la tradición murió mártir hacia 311.
summary.en: A bishop and writer in Lycia who criticized some of Origen's views, especially on the resurrection body. His best-known work, the Symposium, imitates Plato's dialogue to praise virginity; tradition says he died a martyr around 311.

fathers.note: Biography very uncertain: his see (Olympus, Patara or Philippi) and martyrdom (c. 311) rest on Jerome and later tradition.

title.es: Sobre la muerte de los perseguidores
title.en: On the Deaths of the Persecutors

summary.es: Profesor de retórica africano llamado por Diocleciano a Nicomedia, que se convirtió y perdió su cargo durante la gran persecución. Sus Instituciones divinas presentan la fe en latín clásico para lectores cultos, y en su vejez fue tutor de Crispo, hijo de Constantino, en Tréveris.
summary.en: An African teacher of rhetoric summoned by Diocletian to Nicomedia, who converted and lost his post in the Great Persecution. His Divine Institutes present the faith in polished Latin for educated readers, and in old age he tutored Constantine's son Crispus at Trier.

fathers.note: Birth c. 250, death c. 320–325.

summary.es: Obispo de Cesarea de Palestina, conocido como el “padre de la historia eclesiástica”: su Historia conserva numerosos documentos y fragmentos de autores perdidos. Participó en Nicea (325) y simpatizó con Arrio en las primeras etapas, por lo que su ortodoxia se discute y no suele figurar entre los santos en Occidente.
summary.en: Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, known as the "father of church history": his History preserves many documents and fragments of lost authors. He took part in Nicaea (325) and sympathized with Arius in the early stages, so his orthodoxy is debated and he is not usually listed among the saints in the West.

fathers.note: Birth c. 260–265; death 339 or 340. Inclusion as a "Father" varies by tradition; treated here as a key patristic source.

role.es: asceta y escritor siríaco en el Imperio persa
role.en: Syriac ascetic and writer in the Persian Empire

summary.es: Escritor siríaco que vivió bajo el Imperio sasánida, fuera del Imperio romano, posiblemente obispo o monje. Sus veintitrés Demostraciones, fechadas por él mismo entre 337 y 345, muestran un cristianismo semítico poco influido por las controversias griegas de su tiempo.
summary.en: A Syriac writer who lived under the Sasanian Empire, outside the Roman Empire, possibly a bishop or monk. His twenty-three Demonstrations, self-dated between 337 and 345, show a Semitic Christianity little touched by the Greek controversies of his day.

fathers.note: Dates of birth and death unknown; the Demonstrations are dated internally (337, 344, 345). Later tradition links him to the monastery of Mar Mattai near Mosul; city unknown.

summary.es: Obispo de Poitiers y principal defensor del credo niceno en la Galia, desterrado a Frigia por el emperador Constancio II entre 356 y 360. Durante el exilio conoció la teología griega y escribió Sobre la Trinidad, a veces llamado el “Atanasio de Occidente”.
summary.en: Bishop of Poitiers and the leading defender of the Nicene creed in Gaul, exiled to Phrygia by Emperor Constantius II from 356 to 360. In exile he encountered Greek theology and wrote On the Trinity; he is sometimes called the "Athanasius of the West".

fathers.note: Death 367 or 368.

title.en: On the Incarnation of the Word

summary.es: Diácono en Nicea (325) y obispo de Alejandría desde 328, fue el defensor más tenaz del homoousios niceno y sufrió cinco exilios. Su Carta festal 39 (367) es la primera lista conocida que coincide exactamente con los 27 libros del Nuevo Testamento.
summary.en: A deacon at Nicaea (325) and bishop of Alexandria from 328, he was the most tenacious defender of the Nicene homoousios and endured five exiles. His Festal Letter 39 (367) is the first known list that matches exactly the 27 books of the New Testament.

fathers.note: Birth c. 296–298; death 2 May 373 (secure). Date of Against the Pagans / On the Incarnation is disputed (c. 318 before Arius vs. c. 335–337 during first exile).

summary.es: Diácono de Nísibis que se trasladó a Edesa cuando la ciudad pasó a dominio persa en 363. Es el mayor poeta de la tradición siríaca: expresó la teología en himnos ricos en símbolos y tipología, y fue declarado doctor de la Iglesia por la Iglesia católica en 1920.
summary.en: A deacon of Nisibis who moved to Edessa when the city passed to Persian rule in 363. He is the greatest poet of the Syriac tradition, expressing theology in hymns rich in symbol and typology; the Catholic Church named him a Doctor of the Church in 1920.

fathers.note: Birth c. 306; death 9 June 373 (traditional). Many works attributed to "Ephrem" in Greek (Ephraem Graecus) are not his.

summary.es: Uno de los tres Padres Capadocios, obispo de Cesarea desde 370, organizador del monacato oriental y de obras de caridad. Su tratado Sobre el Espíritu Santo defendió que el Espíritu es glorificado junto con el Padre y el Hijo, y su teología preparó el terreno al Concilio de Constantinopla (381).
summary.en: One of the three Cappadocian Fathers, bishop of Caesarea from 370, organizer of Eastern monasticism and of charitable institutions. His treatise On the Holy Spirit argued that the Spirit is glorified together with the Father and the Son, and his theology prepared the ground for the Council of Constantinople (381).

fathers.note: Traditional death 1 January 379; some scholars (Pouchet, Maraval) argue for 377 or 378.

summary.es: Obispo de Jerusalén desde c. 350, desterrado varias veces en las disputas arrianas y presente en el Concilio de Constantinopla (381). Sus catequesis a los candidatos al bautismo son un testimonio detallado de la iniciación cristiana y la liturgia de Jerusalén en el siglo IV.
summary.en: Bishop of Jerusalem from c. 350, exiled several times during the Arian disputes and present at the Council of Constantinople (381). His lectures to baptismal candidates are a detailed witness to Christian initiation and the liturgy of Jerusalem in the fourth century.

fathers.note: Birth c. 313–315; death 386 (traditionally 18 March). The five Mystagogical Catecheses are attributed by some manuscripts and scholars to his successor John II of Jerusalem (bishop 387–417); others hold Cyril wrote them late in life.

summary.es: Padre Capadocio, amigo de Basilio, que dirigió la pequeña comunidad nicena de Constantinopla y presidió por un tiempo el Concilio de 381 antes de renunciar. Sus Discursos teológicos le valieron en Oriente el título de “el Teólogo”, y su carta a Cledonio contiene la fórmula “lo que no fue asumido no fue sanado”.
summary.en: A Cappadocian Father and friend of Basil who led the small Nicene community in Constantinople and briefly presided over the Council of 381 before resigning. His Theological Orations earned him the Eastern title "the Theologian", and his letter to Cledonius contains the formula "what has not been assumed has not been healed".

fathers.note: Birth c. 329–330; death 389 or 390.

summary.es: Hermano menor de Basilio y el más especulativo de los Padres Capadocios, obispo de Nisa y participante en el Concilio de Constantinopla (381). Desarrolló una teología del progreso infinito del alma hacia Dios y de la apocatástasis, que la tradición posterior leyó de formas distintas.
summary.en: Basil's younger brother and the most speculative of the Cappadocian Fathers, bishop of Nyssa and a participant at the Council of Constantinople (381). He developed a theology of the soul's endless progress toward God and of apokatastasis, which later tradition read in different ways.

fathers.note: Birth c. 335; death c. 394–395 or after.

title.es: Sobre los deberes de los ministros
title.en: On the Duties of the Clergy (De officiis)

title.es: Sobre los misterios / Sobre los sacramentos
title.en: On the Mysteries / On the Sacraments

summary.es: Gobernador romano elegido obispo de Milán por aclamación en 374 cuando aún era catecúmeno. Combatió el arrianismo en Occidente, influyó en emperadores como Teodosio y su predicación contribuyó a la conversión de Agustín, a quien bautizó en 387.
summary.en: A Roman governor acclaimed bishop of Milan in 374 while still a catechumen. He opposed Arianism in the West, influenced emperors such as Theodosius, and his preaching contributed to the conversion of Augustine, whom he baptized in 387.

fathers.note: Birth c. 339–340; death 4 April 397 (secure). On the Sacraments (stenographic sermons) was once doubted but is now generally accepted as his.

summary.es: Obispo católico de Milevi, en Numidia, y el primer gran polemista contra el donatismo. Su obra, escrita en respuesta al obispo donatista Parmeniano, defiende la validez de los sacramentos con independencia de la santidad del ministro y la comunión con la sede de Roma.
summary.en: Catholic bishop of Milevis in Numidia and the first major writer against Donatism. His work, a reply to the Donatist bishop Parmenian, defends the validity of the sacraments regardless of the minister’s holiness and communion with the see of Rome.

fathers.note: Death year unknown; he was dead by c. 400 (Augustine refers to him as deceased). Work written c. 366–367 and revised c. 384.

title.es: Sobre el Espíritu Santo (traducción latina de Jerónimo)
title.en: On the Holy Spirit (Latin translation by Jerome)

summary.es: Laico alejandrino ciego desde la infancia que, según la tradición, dirigió la escuela catequética de Alejandría y tuvo como alumnos a Jerónimo y Rufino. Defensor del credo niceno, sus obras fueron condenadas junto con las de Orígenes y Evagrio en 553, y muchas se perdieron hasta el hallazgo de los papiros de Tura en 1941.
summary.en: An Alexandrian layman blind from childhood who, according to tradition, headed the catechetical school of Alexandria and taught Jerome and Rufinus. A defender of the Nicene creed, his works were condemned with those of Origen and Evagrius in 553, and many were lost until the discovery of the Tura papyri in 1941.

fathers.note: Birth c. 313, death c. 398. Authorship of On the Trinity attributed to him is debated.

summary.es: Monje nacido en Palestina y obispo de Salamina en Chipre desde 367, conocido por su celo contra las herejías y contra el origenismo. Su Panarion describe ochenta herejías y conserva información y fragmentos únicos sobre grupos antiguos, aunque su fiabilidad varía según la sección.
summary.en: A Palestinian-born monk and bishop of Salamis in Cyprus from 367, known for his zeal against heresies and against Origenism. His Panarion describes eighty heresies and preserves unique information and fragments on ancient groups, though its reliability varies by section.

fathers.note: Birth c. 310–320; death 403.

title.es: Homilías sobre las cartas de Pablo

summary.es: Predicador de Antioquía, apodado “Boca de Oro” (Crisóstomo), elegido arzobispo de Constantinopla en 398. Sus críticas al lujo de la corte y sus conflictos con Teófilo de Alejandría llevaron a su deposición y destierro, donde murió en 407; la principal liturgia bizantina lleva su nombre.
summary.en: A preacher from Antioch, nicknamed "Golden Mouth" (Chrysostom), chosen archbishop of Constantinople in 398. His criticism of court luxury and conflicts with Theophilus of Alexandria led to his deposition and exile, where he died in 407; the main Byzantine liturgy bears his name.

fathers.note: Birth c. 347–349; death 14 September 407 (secure). The attribution of the Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom in its present form is traditional; its anaphora may go back to him in part.

title.es: Traducción de Sobre los principios de Orígenes
title.en: Translation of Origen's On First Principles

title.es: Historia eclesiástica (traducción y continuación de Eusebio)
title.en: Ecclesiastical History (translation and continuation of Eusebius)

title.es: Comentario al Credo de los Apóstoles

summary.es: Monje y traductor que vivió años en Egipto y Jerusalén y transmitió al Occidente latino muchas obras griegas, sobre todo de Orígenes. Antiguo amigo de Jerónimo, ambos protagonizaron una dura polémica sobre la ortodoxia de Orígenes.
summary.en: A monk and translator who lived for years in Egypt and Jerusalem and passed many Greek works, especially Origen's, to the Latin West. A former friend of Jerome, the two engaged in a bitter dispute over Origen's orthodoxy.

fathers.note: Birth c. 344–345; death 411 in Sicily. Many Origen texts survive only in his (freely adapted) Latin.

summary.es: Erudito nacido en Estridón (Dalmacia), secretario del papa Dámaso en Roma y luego monje en Belén desde 386. Revisó los evangelios latinos y tradujo gran parte del Antiguo Testamento directamente del hebreo, base de la Vulgata, que fue la Biblia del Occidente latino durante más de mil años.
summary.en: A scholar born in Stridon (Dalmatia), secretary to Pope Damasus in Rome and later a monk in Bethlehem from 386. He revised the Latin Gospels and translated most of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew, forming the basis of the Vulgate, the Bible of the Latin West for over a thousand years.

fathers.note: Birth c. 342–347 (debated); death 30 September 420 (traditional, sometimes 419). The Vulgate as a whole includes texts not revised by Jerome (e.g. parts of the NT outside the Gospels).

summary.es: Retórico nacido en Tagaste, convertido en Milán en 386 y obispo de Hipona desde 395/396, es el autor latino más influyente de la Antigüedad cristiana. Sus escritos contra maniqueos, donatistas y pelagianos marcaron la teología occidental de la gracia, la Iglesia y los sacramentos, y fueron invocados tanto por católicos como por reformadores.
summary.en: A rhetorician born in Thagaste, converted in Milan in 386 and bishop of Hippo from 395/396, he is the most influential Latin author of Christian antiquity. His writings against the Manichaeans, Donatists and Pelagians shaped Western theology of grace, the Church and the sacraments, and were invoked by Catholics and Reformers alike.

role.es: monje y fundador monástico en Marsella
role.en: monk and monastic founder in Marseille

summary.es: Monje formado en Belén y en el desierto egipcio, que llevó la espiritualidad monástica oriental al sur de la Galia, donde fundó monasterios en Marsella. Sus obras influyeron en la Regla de Benito; su visión de la gracia y la libertad fue criticada por Próspero de Aquitania y más tarde se la asoció con el llamado “semipelagianismo”.
summary.en: A monk trained in Bethlehem and the Egyptian desert who brought Eastern monastic spirituality to southern Gaul, founding monasteries in Marseille. His works influenced the Rule of Benedict; his view of grace and freedom was criticized by Prosper of Aquitaine and later associated with so-called "Semi-Pelagianism".

fathers.note: Birth c. 360; death c. 435. "Semi-Pelagianism" is a later (16th-c.) label. Venerated as a saint in the East and locally in the West (Marseille).

title.en: Commentary on the Gospel of John

title.es: Tercera carta a Nestorio (con los Doce Anatematismos)
title.en: Third Letter to Nestorius (with the Twelve Anathemas)

summary.es: Patriarca de Alejandría y principal opositor de Nestorio, cuya teología de la unión de la divinidad y la humanidad en la única persona del Verbo dominó el Concilio de Éfeso (431). Es una autoridad común para calcedonianos y ortodoxos orientales, que leen de modo distinto su fórmula “una sola naturaleza encarnada del Verbo de Dios”.
summary.en: Patriarch of Alexandria and the chief opponent of Nestorius, whose theology of the union of divinity and humanity in the one person of the Word dominated the Council of Ephesus (431). He is a shared authority for Chalcedonians and Oriental Orthodox, who read his formula "one incarnate nature of God the Word" differently.

fathers.note: Birth c. 376–378; death 27 June 444 (secure). Accounts of his early episcopate (including the death of Hypatia in 415) are debated; avoid assigning responsibility beyond sources.

summary.es: Monje de la abadía de Lérins, en el sur de la Galia, que escribió bajo el seudónimo de “Peregrino”. Su Conmonitorio propone como criterio de la fe católica “lo que ha sido creído en todas partes, siempre y por todos” y trata del desarrollo legítimo de la doctrina.
summary.en: A monk of the abbey of Lérins in southern Gaul who wrote under the pseudonym "Peregrinus". His Commonitorium proposes as the test of catholic faith "what has been believed everywhere, always and by all" and discusses the legitimate development of doctrine.

fathers.note: Death c. 445, certainly before 450. Some scholars link him to anti-Augustinian circles in Gaul.

summary.es: Obispo de Ravena, entonces sede de la corte imperial de Occidente, desde c. 433. Sus sermones breves y cuidados, conservados en una colección del siglo VIII, le dieron el sobrenombre de “Crisólogo” (palabra de oro); escribió a Eutiques exhortándolo a someterse al obispo de Roma.
summary.en: Bishop of Ravenna, then seat of the Western imperial court, from c. 433. His brief, polished sermons, preserved in an eighth-century collection, earned him the name "Chrysologus" (golden word); he wrote to Eutyches urging him to defer to the bishop of Rome.

fathers.note: Birth c. 380; death c. 450 (traditionally 31 July 450).

title.es: Capítulos sobre la gracia (Indiculus, atribución probable)

summary.es: Laico de Aquitania, defensor de la doctrina agustiniana de la gracia frente a los monjes de Marsella y Lérins, que más tarde trabajó en Roma junto al papa León. Se le atribuye el principio que suele resumirse como lex orandi, lex credendi: la oración de la Iglesia muestra lo que la Iglesia cree.
summary.en: A layman from Aquitaine who defended Augustine's teaching on grace against the monks of Marseille and Lérins, and later worked in Rome alongside Pope Leo. He is credited with the principle usually summarized as lex orandi, lex credendi: the Church's prayer shows what the Church believes.

fathers.note: Birth c. 390; death c. 455. The exact Latin phrase "lex orandi, lex credendi" is a later condensation of "ut legem credendi lex statuat supplicandi" in the Indiculus (Capitula Caelestini), commonly attributed to Prosper.

title.es: Historia religiosa (de los monjes de Siria)
title.en: Religious History (of the monks of Syria)

summary.es: Obispo de Ciro, exégeta e historiador de la tradición antioquena, que criticó los anatematismos de Cirilo y defendió a Nestorio en un primer momento. Depuesto en 449, fue restituido en Calcedonia (451) tras anatematizar a Nestorio; algunos de sus escritos contra Cirilo fueron condenados en 553 (los “Tres Capítulos”).
summary.en: Bishop of Cyrrhus, exegete and historian of the Antiochene tradition, who criticized Cyril's anathemas and initially defended Nestorius. Deposed in 449, he was restored at Chalcedon (451) after anathematizing Nestorius; some of his writings against Cyril were condemned in 553 (the "Three Chapters").

fathers.note: Birth c. 393; death c. 458 (some say c. 460 or 466).

summary.es: Obispo de Roma de 440 a 461, cuyo Tomo a Flaviano expuso las dos naturalezas de Cristo en una sola persona y fue recibido en el Concilio de Calcedonia (451). Desarrolló una teología del primado romano basada en Pedro y, según la tradición, negoció con Atila (452) y con los vándalos (455).
summary.en: Bishop of Rome from 440 to 461, whose Tome to Flavian set out the two natures of Christ in one person and was received at the Council of Chalcedon (451). He developed a theology of Roman primacy grounded in Peter and, according to tradition, negotiated with Attila (452) and the Vandals (455).

fathers.note: Birth c. 400; death 10 November 461 (secure).

role.es: corpus anónimo atribuido a Dionisio Areopagita
role.en: anonymous corpus attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite

summary.es: Conjunto de tratados escritos por un autor anónimo, probablemente un monje sirio influido por el neoplatonismo de Proclo, que se presenta como Dionisio, el converso de Pablo en Atenas (Hch 17,34). Influyó profundamente en la teología mística y litúrgica de Oriente y Occidente; su autoría apostólica fue cuestionada ya en el siglo VI y abandonada en la era moderna.
summary.en: A set of treatises by an anonymous author, probably a Syrian monk influenced by Proclus' Neoplatonism, who presents himself as Dionysius, Paul's convert in Athens (Acts 17:34). It deeply influenced mystical and liturgical theology in East and West; its apostolic authorship was questioned already in the sixth century and abandoned in the modern era.

fathers.note: Kind "work": `died` = conventional composition year. Written after Proclus (d. 485) and before first citation (c. 518–528, by Severus of Antioch; debated at the 532 Constantinople colloquy).

summary.es: Monje de Lérins y obispo de Arlés desde 502, el pastor más influyente de la Galia en su tiempo. Presidió el Segundo Concilio de Orange (529), que adoptó una versión moderada de la doctrina agustiniana de la gracia, y sus sermones prácticos circularon ampliamente en la Edad Media.
summary.en: A monk of Lérins and bishop of Arles from 502, the most influential pastor in Gaul in his day. He presided over the Second Council of Orange (529), which adopted a moderate version of Augustine's doctrine of grace, and his practical sermons circulated widely in the Middle Ages.

fathers.note: Birth c. 468–470; death 27 August 542 (secure).

title.es: Moralia in Iob (Comentario moral a Job)

summary.es: Prefecto de Roma convertido en monje y elegido obispo de Roma en 590, en una Italia golpeada por la peste y la invasión lombarda. Su Regla pastoral fue un manual clásico para obispos, envió la misión de Agustín de Canterbury a Inglaterra (596) y su obra marcó la transición de la Antigüedad a la Edad Media latina.
summary.en: A former prefect of Rome who became a monk and was elected bishop of Rome in 590, in an Italy hit by plague and Lombard invasion. His Pastoral Rule became a classic handbook for bishops, he sent Augustine of Canterbury's mission to England (596), and his work marks the transition from Antiquity to the Latin Middle Ages.

fathers.note: Birth c. 540; death 12 March 604 (secure). Authenticity of the Dialogues has been questioned (F. Clark) but most scholars accept them.

summary.es: Obispo de Sevilla desde c. 600, sucesor de su hermano Leandro, en la Hispania visigoda ya convertida al catolicismo. Sus Etimologías, una enciclopedia del saber antiguo, fueron uno de los libros más copiados de la Edad Media; presidió el IV Concilio de Toledo (633).
summary.en: Bishop of Seville from c. 600, succeeding his brother Leander, in Visigothic Spain after its conversion to Catholicism. His Etymologies, an encyclopedia of ancient learning, was one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages; he presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo (633).

fathers.note: Birth c. 560; death 4 April 636 (secure).

summary.es: Monje y patriarca de Jerusalén, el primer gran opositor del monoenergismo, la doctrina de una sola “energía” en Cristo promovida como fórmula de unión. Le tocó entregar Jerusalén al califa Umar tras el asedio árabe (637/638) y murió poco después.
summary.en: A monk and patriarch of Jerusalem, the first major opponent of monoenergism, the doctrine of a single "energy" in Christ promoted as a formula of union. He surrendered Jerusalem to Caliph Umar after the Arab siege (637/638) and died shortly afterward.

fathers.note: Birth c. 560; death 11 March 638 (traditional). The Spiritual Meadow is by John Moschus; Sophronius was his companion and probably completed/edited it.

summary.es: Monje y teólogo que defendió que Cristo tiene dos voluntades, divina y humana, frente al monotelismo apoyado por la corte imperial. Fue juzgado en Constantinopla y mutilado (lengua y mano derecha) antes de morir en el exilio en 662; el Tercer Concilio de Constantinopla (680–681) confirmó su postura.
summary.en: A monk and theologian who argued that Christ has two wills, divine and human, against the monothelitism backed by the imperial court. He was tried in Constantinople and mutilated (tongue and right hand) before dying in exile in 662; the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681) vindicated his position.

fathers.note: Birth c. 580. Origin disputed: the Greek Life says Constantinople aristocracy; a hostile Syriac Life says Palestine (Hesfin). Death 13 August 662 (secure).

role.es: obispo de Nínive y monje de la Iglesia del Oriente
role.en: bishop of Nineveh and monk of the Church of the East

summary.es: Monje nacido en Beth Qatraye (Arabia oriental), consagrado obispo de Nínive hacia 676 por el católicos de la Iglesia del Oriente, cargo que dejó a los pocos meses para retirarse a la vida solitaria. Sus escritos sobre la oración y la misericordia de Dios, traducidos al griego en el siglo IX, son muy leídos en las tradiciones ortodoxa y ortodoxa oriental, además de la suya propia.
summary.en: A monk born in Beth Qatraye (eastern Arabia), consecrated bishop of Nineveh around 676 by the catholicos of the Church of the East, a post he left after a few months for solitary life. His writings on prayer and God's mercy, translated into Greek in the ninth century, are widely read in the Eastern and Oriental Orthodox traditions as well as his own.

fathers.note: Birth c. 613 and death c. 700 are estimates. He belonged to the Church of the East (which did not accept Ephesus 431), yet is venerated as a saint in Eastern Orthodoxy — note this neutrally.

title.es: Sobre el cómputo del tiempo (De temporum ratione)
title.en: The Reckoning of Time (De temporum ratione)
Ecclesiastical History of the English People

summary.es: Monje del monasterio de Wearmouth-Jarrow en Northumbria, autor de comentarios bíblicos, obras científicas e historia. Su Historia eclesiástica es la fuente principal sobre la cristianización de Inglaterra y popularizó el cómputo de los años “desde la Encarnación” (anno Domini).
summary.en: A monk of the Wearmouth-Jarrow monastery in Northumbria, author of biblical commentaries, scientific works and history. His Ecclesiastical History is the main source on the Christianization of England and popularized dating years "from the Incarnation" (anno Domini).

fathers.note: Birth c. 672–673; death 26 May 735 (secure). Often placed at the edge of the patristic era; the Catholic Church named him a Doctor of the Church in 1899.

summary.es: Monje nacido en Damasco, formado en Jerusalén y luego arzobispo de Gortina en Creta, conocido como predicador e himnógrafo. Su Gran Canon, de unas 250 estrofas, se canta todavía en la Cuaresma bizantina; en 712 aceptó brevemente el monotelismo en un sínodo y luego se retractó.
summary.en: A monk born in Damascus, trained in Jerusalem and later archbishop of Gortyna in Crete, known as a preacher and hymnographer. His Great Canon, of some 250 stanzas, is still sung in Byzantine Lent; in 712 he briefly accepted monothelitism at a synod and later recanted.

fathers.note: Birth c. 650–660; death 4 July of 712, 726 or 740 (year disputed; 740 conventional). Date of the Great Canon unknown.

title.es: Historia eclesiástica y contemplación mística (sobre la Divina Liturgia)
title.en: Ecclesiastical History and Mystical Contemplation (On the Divine Liturgy)

summary.es: Patriarca de Constantinopla que se opuso a la política iconoclasta del emperador León III y fue obligado a renunciar en 730. Su comentario a la Divina Liturgia fue durante siglos la explicación de referencia en el mundo bizantino, y el Segundo Concilio de Nicea (787) honró su memoria.
summary.en: Patriarch of Constantinople who opposed Emperor Leo III's iconoclast policy and was forced to resign in 730. His commentary on the Divine Liturgy was for centuries the standard explanation in the Byzantine world, and the Second Council of Nicaea (787) honored his memory.

fathers.note: Birth c. 634; death c. 740 (some sources 733). Authorship of the liturgical commentary in its received form is generally accepted with interpolations.

role.es: monje y presbítero de Mar Saba
role.en: monk and priest of Mar Saba

title.en: Three Treatises on the Divine Images

title.es: Fuente del conocimiento (incl. Exposición exacta de la fe ortodoxa)
title.en: The Fount of Knowledge (incl. An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith)

summary.es: Funcionario cristiano en la administración del califato omeya en Damasco que se hizo monje en el monasterio de Mar Saba, cerca de Jerusalén. Defendió la veneración de las imágenes contra el iconoclasmo bizantino y su Exposición de la fe ortodoxa sintetizó la teología patrística griega; suele considerarse el último de los Padres de la Iglesia.
summary.en: A Christian official in the administration of the Umayyad caliphate in Damascus who became a monk at the Mar Saba monastery near Jerusalem. He defended the veneration of images against Byzantine iconoclasm, and his Exposition of the Orthodox Faith synthesized Greek patristic theology; he is often regarded as the last of the Church Fathers.

fathers.note: Birth c. 675–676; death traditionally 4 December 749, some argue 753–754. The iconoclast Council of Hieria (754) anathematized him, suggesting he was dead by then.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: No se cuenta entre los concilios ecuménicos; todas las tradiciones lo consideran una asamblea apostólica y un modelo para los concilios posteriores.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Not counted among the ecumenical councils; all traditions regard it as an apostolic assembly and a model for later councils.

convokedBy.es: Los apóstoles y presbíteros de Jerusalén (Hechos 15), con Pedro, Santiago, Pablo y Bernabé
convokedBy.en: The apostles and elders in Jerusalem (Acts 15), with Peter, James, Paul and Barnabas

decisions.es: Resolvió que los gentiles que creían en Cristo no debían circuncidarse ni asumir toda la ley mosaica para ser salvos. Mediante una carta (el “decreto apostólico”) les pidió abstenerse de lo sacrificado a los ídolos, de la sangre, de lo estrangulado y de la inmoralidad sexual (Hch 15:28–29).
decisions.en: Decided that Gentile believers did not need to be circumcised or take on the whole Mosaic law in order to be saved. In a letter (the “apostolic decree”) it asked them to abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled and from sexual immorality (Acts 15:28–29).

councils.note: Date conventional (c. 48–50). How Acts 15 relates to Paul's account in Galatians 2:1–10 is debated by scholars.

name.es: Sínodo de Antioquía contra Pablo de Samosata
name.en: Synod of Antioch against Paul of Samosata

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna (sínodo local)
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None (local synod)

decisions.es: Condenó y depuso a Pablo de Samosata, obispo de Antioquía, cuya cristología se suele clasificar como monarquianismo dinámico (Jesús como hombre en quien habitaba el Logos o la sabiduría de Dios). Según fuentes posteriores, el sínodo rechazó el término homoousios en el sentido en que lo usaba Pablo. Pablo se negó a dejar la sede hasta que el emperador Aureliano intervino (c. 272).
decisions.en: Condemned and deposed Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, whose Christology is usually classed as dynamic monarchianism (Jesus as a man indwelt by God's Word or Wisdom). According to later sources, the synod rejected the term homoousios in the sense Paul used it. Paul refused to leave the see until Emperor Aurelian intervened (c. 272).

councils.note: Exact date and number of sessions uncertain (264–269). The rejection of homoousios is reported by 4th-century writers (Athanasius, Hilary, Basil) and its exact sense is debated.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna (sínodo local hispano)
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None (local Hispanic synod)

place.es: Iliberris (Elvira), cerca de la actual Granada, Hispania

decisions.es: Se le atribuyen 81 cánones de disciplina muy severa: penitencias largas o exclusión de la comunión para la idolatría, el adulterio y otros pecados graves. El canon 33 exige a obispos, presbíteros y diáconos abstenerse de sus esposas (el canon más antiguo conocido sobre continencia clerical) y el canon 36 prohíbe pinturas en las iglesias “para que lo que se venera y adora no se pinte en las paredes”.
decisions.en: 81 canons of very strict discipline are attributed to it: long penances or exclusion from communion for idolatry, adultery and other grave sins. Canon 33 requires bishops, presbyters and deacons to abstain from their wives (the earliest known canon on clerical continence), and canon 36 forbids pictures in churches “so that what is venerated and adored is not painted on the walls.”

councils.note: Date and integrity disputed. Maurice Meigne argued that only the first 21 canons belong to Elvira and the rest were added to the collection later. The meaning of canon 36 has been contested between Catholic and Protestant scholars since the Reformation.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna (concilio occidental)
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None (Western council)

decisions.es: Convocado por Constantino tras la apelación de los donatistas, ratificó la decisión romana de 313 contra ellos y a favor de Ceciliano, obispo de Cartago. Estableció que quienes habían sido bautizados por herejes en el nombre de la Trinidad no debían ser rebautizados, y que la Pascua se celebrara el mismo día en todo el mundo. Asistieron obispos de Britania (entre ellos los de York y Londres). Se conservan unos 22 cánones.
decisions.en: Called by Constantine after the Donatists appealed, it upheld the Roman decision of 313 against them and in favor of Caecilian, bishop of Carthage. It ruled that those baptized by heretics in the name of the Trinity should not be rebaptized, and that Easter be kept on the same day throughout the world. Bishops from Britain attended (among them those of York and London). About 22 canons survive.

councils.note: Canon count varies slightly between manuscript collections (usually given as 22).

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Iglesia católica, Iglesia ortodoxa, Iglesias ortodoxas orientales e Iglesia del Oriente; muchas iglesias protestantes aceptan su credo como fiel a la Escritura.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church, Eastern Orthodox Church, Oriental Orthodox Churches and the Church of the East; many Protestant churches accept its creed as faithful to Scripture.

decisions.es: Condenó la enseñanza de Arrio de que el Hijo es una criatura que tuvo comienzo (“hubo un tiempo en que no era”) y promulgó el Credo niceno, que confiesa al Hijo “consustancial” (homoousios) al Padre. Fijó criterios para una fecha común de la Pascua, trató el cisma meleciano de Egipto y emitió 20 cánones (por ejemplo, el canon 6 sobre las prerrogativas de Alejandría, Roma y Antioquía). Asistieron unos 250–300 obispos; la tradición habla de 318.
decisions.en: Condemned Arius' teaching that the Son is a creature who had a beginning (“there was when he was not”) and issued the Nicene Creed, which confesses the Son “of one substance” (homoousios) with the Father. It set principles for a common date of Easter, dealt with the Meletian schism in Egypt and issued 20 canons (e.g. canon 6 on the prerogatives of Alexandria, Rome and Antioch). Some 250–300 bishops attended; tradition gives 318.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Iglesia católica, Iglesia ortodoxa, Iglesias ortodoxas orientales e Iglesia del Oriente; muchas iglesias protestantes aceptan su credo. Fue un concilio solo de obispos orientales y su carácter ecuménico se reconoció después, sobre todo en Calcedonia (451).
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church, Eastern Orthodox Church, Oriental Orthodox Churches and the Church of the East; many Protestant churches accept its creed. Only Eastern bishops attended; its ecumenical standing was recognized later, especially at Chalcedon (451).

decisions.es: Reafirmó la fe de Nicea y se le atribuye el Credo niceno-constantinopolitano, que amplía el artículo sobre el Espíritu Santo: “Señor y dador de vida, que procede del Padre, que con el Padre y el Hijo recibe una misma adoración y gloria”. Condenó a los pneumatómacos (macedonianos), a los apolinaristas, a los eunomianos y otros grupos. El canon 3 dio al obispo de Constantinopla el primer lugar de honor después del de Roma, “por ser la nueva Roma”. Unos 150 obispos.
decisions.en: Reaffirmed the faith of Nicaea and is credited with the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, which expands the article on the Holy Spirit: “the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified.” It condemned the Pneumatomachi (Macedonians), Apollinarians, Eunomians and other groups. Canon 3 gave the bishop of Constantinople the first place of honor after the bishop of Rome, “because it is New Rome.” About 150 bishops.

councils.note: 4 canons in the Latin tradition, 7 in the Greek (canons 5–7 probably come from a synod of 382 and later practice). The creed's text is first attested in the acts of Chalcedon (451). Rome accepted the creed but long resisted canon 3.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna (sínodo local)
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None (local synod)

decisions.es: Sínodo occidental reunido tras el concilio de Constantinopla de 381, con Jerónimo presente como secretario de Dámaso. Tradicionalmente se le atribuye una lista de los libros canónicos del Antiguo y del Nuevo Testamento (incluidos los deuterocanónicos) conservada en el llamado Decreto gelasiano, pero esa atribución está muy discutida.
decisions.en: A Western synod held after the Council of Constantinople of 381, with Jerome present as Damasus' secretary. Tradition attributes to it a list of the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments (including the deuterocanonical books) preserved in the so-called Gelasian Decree, but that attribution is heavily disputed.

councils.note: The 'Damasine list' survives only inside the Decretum Gelasianum. Ernst von Dobschütz (1912) argued the Decree is a pseudonymous 6th-century compilation (c. 519–553) and not a decree of Damasus or Gelasius; others (e.g. C. H. Turner) thought the canon-list chapter could preserve 382 material. The Tome of Damasus (anathemas against Apollinarians, Macedonians and others) is linked to Roman synods of c. 377–382; its exact date is uncertain.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna (sínodo regional africano)
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None (regional African synod)

place.es: Hipona (Hippo Regius), norte de África (actual Annaba, Argelia)
place.en: Hippo Regius, North Africa (modern Annaba, Algeria)

convokedBy.es: Aurelio, obispo de Cartago (concilio plenario africano)
convokedBy.en: Aurelius, bishop of Carthage (plenary African council)

decisions.es: Primer concilio conocido que aprobó una lista de libros canónicos coincidente con el canon católico posterior, incluidos los deuterocanónicos (Tobías, Judit, Sabiduría, Sirácida, Macabeos) y los 27 libros del Nuevo Testamento. También dictó normas de disciplina clerical. Agustín, entonces presbítero, pronunció ante los obispos su discurso Sobre la fe y el símbolo.
decisions.en: The first known council to approve a list of canonical books matching the later Catholic canon, including the deuterocanonical books (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Maccabees) and the 27 books of the New Testament. It also enacted rules of clerical discipline. Augustine, then a presbyter, delivered his address On Faith and the Creed to the bishops.

councils.note: Held 8 October 393. The acts are lost; its canons survive only in a summary (Breviarium Hipponense) read and adopted at Carthage in 397. The list itself also asked that it be confirmed by the 'Church across the sea' (Rome).

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna (concilio regional africano)
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None (regional African council)

decisions.es: Reunido el 28 de agosto de 397, con la presencia de Agustín, adoptó el resumen de los cánones de Hipona (393), incluida la lista de libros canónicos del Antiguo y Nuevo Testamento con los deuterocanónicos.
decisions.en: Meeting on 28 August 397, with Augustine present, it adopted the summary of the canons of Hippo (393), including the list of canonical books of the Old and New Testaments with the deuterocanonical books.

councils.note: The 397 list is commonly reported as counting 'thirteen epistles of Paul, and one of the same to the Hebrews', whereas the 419 code reads 'fourteen epistles of Paul'; the wording reflects lingering debate over Hebrews' authorship, not its canonicity. Numbering of the Carthaginian councils varies between editions.

name.es: Concilio de Cartago contra el pelagianismo

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna (concilio regional africano), aunque sus cánones fueron respaldados por el papa Zósimo en su Epistola tractoria y recibidos ampliamente en Occidente.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None (regional African council), though its canons were backed by Pope Zosimus in his Epistola tractoria and widely received in the West.

decisions.es: El 1 de mayo de 418 más de 200 obispos aprobaron cánones contra las tesis de Pelagio y Celestio: Adán no habría muerto si no hubiera pecado; los niños se bautizan para la remisión del pecado original; la gracia no solo perdona pecados pasados sino que ayuda a no pecar; y nadie en esta vida está sin pecado. Los cánones se incorporaron después al Código de la Iglesia africana (419).
decisions.en: On 1 May 418 over 200 bishops approved canons against the views of Pelagius and Caelestius: Adam would not have died had he not sinned; infants are baptized for the remission of original sin; grace does not only forgive past sins but helps us not to sin; and no one in this life is without sin. The canons were later included in the Code of the African Church (419).

councils.note: Usually counted as 8 canons (some collections give 9, with a disputed canon on unbaptized infants).

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna como concilio ecuménico; su código canónico fue recibido en el derecho canónico bizantino y confirmado por el Concilio de Trullo (692).
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None as an ecumenical council; its canon code was received into Byzantine canon law and confirmed by the Council in Trullo (692).

decisions.es: Reunido el 25 y el 30 de mayo de 419 con 217 obispos, compiló el Código de cánones de la Iglesia africana (138 cánones en la versión latina, 135 en la griega) a partir de concilios anteriores, repitiendo la lista de libros canónicos. Trató también el caso del presbítero Apiario, apelado ante Roma, y defendió la potestad de los obispos africanos para resolver sus propias causas sin apelaciones “al otro lado del mar”.
decisions.en: Meeting on 25 and 30 May 419 with 217 bishops, it compiled the Code of Canons of the African Church (138 canons in Latin, 135 in Greek) from earlier councils, repeating the list of canonical books. It also handled the case of the presbyter Apiarius, who had appealed to Rome, and defended the African bishops' right to settle their own cases without appeals “across the sea.”

councils.note: The code is a compilation; dating individual canons to particular earlier councils is not always certain.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Iglesia católica, Iglesia ortodoxa e Iglesias ortodoxas orientales; no lo acepta la Iglesia del Oriente. Muchas iglesias protestantes aceptan su enseñanza cristológica.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church, Eastern Orthodox Church and Oriental Orthodox Churches; not accepted by the Church of the East. Many Protestant churches accept its Christological teaching.

convokedBy.es: El emperador Teodosio II (con Valentiniano III)

decisions.es: Presidido por Cirilo de Alejandría, depuso a Nestorio, obispo de Constantinopla, y aprobó la segunda carta de Cirilo a Nestorio como conforme a Nicea. Confesó que el Verbo se unió a la carne en una sola persona, de modo que María es Theotokos (“Madre de Dios”). El canon 7 prohibió componer otro credo distinto del de Nicea y otros cánones condenaron a Celestio y a los pelagianos. Los obispos antioquenos, con Juan de Antioquía, celebraron una asamblea rival; la reconciliación llegó con la Fórmula de unión de 433.
decisions.en: Presided over by Cyril of Alexandria, it deposed Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, and approved Cyril's second letter to Nestorius as agreeing with Nicaea. It confessed that the Word united flesh to himself in one person, so that Mary is Theotokos (“God-bearer, Mother of God”). Canon 7 forbade composing a creed other than that of Nicaea, and other canons condemned Caelestius and the Pelagians. The Antiochene bishops under John of Antioch held a rival assembly; reconciliation came with the Formula of Reunion of 433.

councils.note: Whether the council formally adopted Cyril's Twelve Anathemas (which were read into the acts) is debated. Canon 8 recognized the autonomy of the Church of Cyprus.

name.es: Segundo Concilio de Éfeso (“Latrocinio de Éfeso”)

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Convocado como concilio general, fue anulado por Calcedonia (451) y no se cuenta como ecuménico en ninguna tradición. Las Iglesias ortodoxas orientales veneran a Dióscoro como santo y valoran ese concilio de forma distinta que las Iglesias calcedonianas.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Called as a general council, it was annulled by Chalcedon (451) and is not counted as ecumenical in any tradition. The Oriental Orthodox Churches venerate Dioscorus as a saint and assess the council differently from the Chalcedonian churches.

decisions.es: Presidido por Dióscoro de Alejandría, rehabilitó al monje Eutiques y depuso a Flaviano de Constantinopla, a Domno de Antioquía, a Teodoreto de Ciro e Ibas de Edesa. No se permitió leer el Tomo del papa León. Flaviano murió poco después a causa del maltrato sufrido, y León llamó a la asamblea latrocinium (“latrocinio”).
decisions.en: Presided over by Dioscorus of Alexandria, it rehabilitated the monk Eutyches and deposed Flavian of Constantinople, Domnus of Antioch, Theodoret of Cyrrhus and Ibas of Edessa. Pope Leo's Tome was not allowed to be read. Flavian died soon after from mistreatment, and Leo called the assembly a latrocinium (“robbery”).

councils.note: Accounts of violence come mainly from Chalcedonian sources; Oriental Orthodox historiography reads the events and Dioscorus' role differently.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Iglesia católica e Iglesia ortodoxa; muchas iglesias protestantes aceptan su definición cristológica. Las Iglesias ortodoxas orientales lo rechazan (aceptan solo los tres primeros concilios).
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church and Eastern Orthodox Church; many Protestant churches accept its Christological definition. The Oriental Orthodox Churches reject it (they accept only the first three councils).

place.es: Calcedonia, frente a Constantinopla (actual Kadıköy, Estambul)
place.en: Chalcedon, across from Constantinople (modern Kadıköy, Istanbul)

convokedBy.es: El emperador Marciano (con la emperatriz Pulqueria)

decisions.es: Anuló el concilio de 449, depuso a Dióscoro y condenó a Eutiques. Recibió el Tomo de León y las cartas de Cirilo, y promulgó la Definición de Calcedonia: un solo y mismo Cristo, Hijo, Señor, “reconocido en dos naturalezas, sin confusión, sin cambio, sin división, sin separación”, que concurren en una sola persona (prósopon) e hipóstasis. Emitió 27 cánones disciplinarios más el canon 28, que otorgó a Constantinopla privilegios iguales a los de Roma como “nueva Roma”; el papa León rechazó ese canon. Asistieron unos 350–370 obispos (la tradición dice 630).
decisions.en: Annulled the council of 449, deposed Dioscorus and condemned Eutyches. It received Leo's Tome and Cyril's letters and issued the Chalcedonian Definition: one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, “acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation,” concurring in one person (prosopon) and hypostasis. It issued 27 disciplinary canons plus canon 28, which granted Constantinople privileges equal to Rome's as “New Rome”; Pope Leo rejected that canon. Some 350–370 bishops attended (tradition says 630).

councils.note: Canon count: 27 + canon 28 (disputed, not accepted by Rome); canons 29–30 are extracts from the minutes added in some collections. The Oriental Orthodox regard the Definition as conceding too much to Nestorian language and keep Cyril's formula 'one incarnate nature of God the Word' (miaphysitism); they reject the label 'monophysite'.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna (sínodo local galo); aprobado por el papa Bonifacio II (531), lo que le dio gran autoridad en la Iglesia católica. Muchos protestantes lo citan con aprecio.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None (local Gallic synod); approved by Pope Boniface II (531), which gave it great authority in the Catholic Church. Many Protestants cite it approvingly.

decisions.es: El 3 de julio de 529, catorce obispos aprobaron 25 cánones sobre la gracia: incluso el comienzo de la fe (initium fidei) es don de la gracia y no fruto del libre albedrío caído; la gracia precede a toda obra buena. A la vez rechazó con anatema que Dios predestine a alguien al mal. Sus cánones se perdieron hacia el siglo X y se recuperaron y publicaron en 1543.
decisions.en: On 3 July 529 fourteen bishops approved 25 canons on grace: even the beginning of faith (initium fidei) is a gift of grace and not the fruit of fallen free will; grace precedes every good work. At the same time it anathematized the idea that God predestines anyone to evil. Its canons were lost around the 10th century and recovered and published in 1543.

councils.note: 'Semi-Pelagianism' is a later (16th–17th c.) label for the position of John Cassian and Faustus of Riez; some historians prefer 'Massilianism'.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Iglesia católica e Iglesia ortodoxa. Las Iglesias ortodoxas orientales no lo aceptan; muchas iglesias protestantes dan menos peso a los concilios quinto a séptimo.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church and Eastern Orthodox Church. The Oriental Orthodox Churches do not accept it; many Protestant churches give less weight to the fifth to seventh councils.

decisions.es: Condenó los “Tres Capítulos”: la persona y los escritos de Teodoro de Mopsuestia, ciertos escritos de Teodoreto contra Cirilo y la carta de Ibas de Edesa a Mari. Sus 14 anatemas interpretan Calcedonia en sentido cirílico (por ejemplo, “uno de la Trinidad padeció en la carne”), en un intento de reconciliar a los adversarios de Calcedonia. El papa Vigilio, presente en Constantinopla, se negó a asistir pero luego aprobó las decisiones (553–554), lo que provocó en Occidente el cisma de los Tres Capítulos.
decisions.en: Condemned the “Three Chapters”: the person and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain writings of Theodoret against Cyril, and the letter of Ibas of Edessa to Mari. Its 14 anathemas interpret Chalcedon in a Cyrilline sense (e.g. “one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh”), in an attempt to reconcile Chalcedon's opponents. Pope Vigilius, who was in Constantinople, refused to attend but later approved the decisions (553–554), which triggered the Three Chapters schism in the West.

councils.note: Issued anathemas but no disciplinary canons. Fifteen anathemas against Origenism are attached to it in some sources; whether they were approved by the council itself or by a session just before its formal opening is debated. Origen is also named in anathema 11.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna (concilio del reino visigodo)
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None (council of the Visigothic kingdom)

decisions.es: Selló la conversión del rey Recaredo y del pueblo visigodo del arrianismo a la fe nicena. Presidido por Leandro de Sevilla, con unos 72 obispos, emitió 23 cánones. El credo que profesó incluía que el Espíritu Santo procede “del Padre y del Hijo” (Filioque), uno de los primeros usos conciliares de esa fórmula, que más tarde fue una de las causas de la separación entre Oriente y Occidente.
decisions.en: Sealed the conversion of King Reccared and the Visigothic people from Arianism to the Nicene faith. Presided over by Leander of Seville, with about 72 bishops, it issued 23 canons. The creed it professed said the Holy Spirit proceeds “from the Father and the Son” (Filioque), one of the earliest conciliar uses of the formula, which later became one of the causes of the East–West separation.

councils.note: Whether 'Filioque' stood in the original text of the creed recited at Toledo III or was added in later manuscripts has been debated, though the council's own profession of faith clearly teaches procession from Father and Son.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna como concilio ecuménico; su doctrina fue confirmada por el Tercer Concilio de Constantinopla (680–681).
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None as an ecumenical council; its teaching was confirmed by the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681).

decisions.es: En cinco sesiones (octubre de 649) condenó el monotelismo y rechazó dos documentos imperiales: la Ecthesis de Heraclio y el Typos de Constante II, que prohibía discutir sobre una o dos voluntades. Sus 20 cánones afirman en Cristo dos voluntades y dos operaciones naturales. Máximo el Confesor fue su principal inspirador teológico. Constante II hizo arrestar a Martín y a Máximo; Martín murió desterrado en Crimea en 655.
decisions.en: In five sessions (October 649) it condemned Monothelitism and rejected two imperial documents: Heraclius' Ekthesis and Constans II's Typos, which forbade discussing one or two wills. Its 20 canons affirm two natural wills and two natural operations in Christ. Maximus the Confessor was its main theological architect. Constans II had Martin and Maximus arrested; Martin died in exile in Crimea in 655.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Iglesia católica e Iglesia ortodoxa. Las Iglesias ortodoxas orientales no lo aceptan.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church and Eastern Orthodox Church. The Oriental Orthodox Churches do not accept it.

place.es: Constantinopla (sala abovedada o “Trullo” del palacio imperial)
place.en: Constantinople (domed hall or “Trullo” of the imperial palace)

decisions.es: Del 7 de noviembre de 680 al 16 de septiembre de 681. Recibió la carta del papa Agatón y definió que en Cristo hay dos voluntades naturales y dos operaciones naturales, divina y humana, sin oposición: la voluntad humana sigue y se somete a la divina. Condenó como monotelitas a Sergio, Pirro, Pablo y Pedro de Constantinopla, a Ciro de Alejandría, a Macario de Antioquía y al papa Honorio I.
decisions.en: From 7 November 680 to 16 September 681. It received Pope Agatho's letter and defined that Christ has two natural wills and two natural operations, divine and human, not opposed: the human will follows and is subject to the divine. It condemned as Monothelites Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul and Peter of Constantinople, Cyrus of Alexandria, Macarius of Antioch and Pope Honorius I.

councils.note: Issued no disciplinary canons (supplied later by the Council in Trullo, 692). The meaning of Honorius' condemnation was much debated, especially around Vatican I (1870).

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: La Iglesia ortodoxa considera sus cánones parte del sexto concilio ecuménico y de autoridad ecuménica. La Iglesia católica no lo cuenta como ecuménico; Roma nunca lo aceptó en bloque.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: The Eastern Orthodox Church regards its canons as part of the sixth ecumenical council and of ecumenical authority. The Catholic Church does not count it as ecumenical; Rome never accepted it as a whole.

place.es: Constantinopla (sala abovedada o “Trullo” del palacio imperial)
place.en: Constantinople (domed hall or “Trullo” of the imperial palace)

decisions.es: Llamado “quinisexto” porque completó con legislación disciplinaria los concilios quinto y sexto, que no habían emitido cánones. Promulgó 102 cánones y confirmó colecciones anteriores (incluidos los 85 Cánones apostólicos y los concilios de Cartago). Permitió que los presbíteros y diáconos casados antes de su ordenación siguieran viviendo con sus esposas (canon 13), exigió el celibato a los obispos (canon 12), renovó el rango de Constantinopla (canon 36) y criticó algunas costumbres romanas, como el ayuno del sábado (canon 55).
decisions.en: Called “Quinisext” (fifth-sixth) because it supplied disciplinary legislation for the fifth and sixth councils, which had issued no canons. It enacted 102 canons and confirmed earlier collections (including the 85 Apostolic Canons and the councils of Carthage). It allowed presbyters and deacons married before ordination to continue living with their wives (canon 13), required bishops to be celibate (canon 12), renewed Constantinople's rank (canon 36) and criticized some Roman customs, such as fasting on Saturdays (canon 55).

councils.note: Pope Sergius I refused to sign. Later popes (often cited: John VIII, late 9th c.) accepted the canons not contrary to Roman practice; the extent and date of that partial acceptance is uncertain.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Iglesia católica e Iglesia ortodoxa. Las Iglesias ortodoxas orientales no lo cuentan entre sus concilios. La mayoría de las iglesias protestantes no aceptan su enseñanza sobre la veneración de imágenes.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church and Eastern Orthodox Church. The Oriental Orthodox Churches do not count it among their councils. Most Protestant churches do not accept its teaching on the veneration of images.

convokedBy.es: La emperatriz Irene (regente de Constantino VI), con el patriarca Tarasio
convokedBy.en: Empress Irene (regent for Constantine VI), with Patriarch Tarasius

decisions.es: Del 24 de septiembre al 23 de octubre de 787, con legados del papa Adriano I. Restableció la veneración de los íconos: la veneración de honor (proskýnesis) que se tributa a la imagen pasa a su prototipo, mientras que la adoración (latreía) se debe solo a Dios. Anuló el concilio iconoclasta de Hieria (754) y emitió 22 cánones. Un primer intento en Constantinopla (786) había sido disuelto por soldados iconoclastas.
decisions.en: From 24 September to 23 October 787, with legates of Pope Hadrian I. It restored the veneration of icons: the honorific veneration (proskynesis) given to an image passes to its prototype, while worship (latreia) is due to God alone. It annulled the iconoclast Council of Hieria (754) and issued 22 canons. A first attempt in Constantinople (786) had been broken up by iconoclast soldiers.

councils.note: Iconoclasm returned in 815 and ended definitively in 843 (the 'Triumph of Orthodoxy'). In the West the council was initially received through a faulty Latin translation (see Frankfurt 794).

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Ninguna (sínodo franco)
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: None (Frankish synod)

decisions.es: En junio de 794, con legados del papa Adriano I, condenó el adopcionismo hispano de Elipando de Toledo y Félix de Urgel (Cristo, en cuanto hombre, sería Hijo adoptivo). También rechazó lo que entendía como decisión de Nicea II: admitió que las imágenes son útiles para instruir, pero negó que deban recibir veneración. Sus resoluciones se recogen en un capitular de 56 capítulos.
decisions.en: In June 794, with legates of Pope Hadrian I, it condemned the Spanish Adoptionism of Elipandus of Toledo and Felix of Urgell (that Christ, as man, is the adoptive Son). It also rejected what it understood Nicaea II to have decided: it allowed that images are useful for instruction but denied they should be venerated. Its rulings are gathered in a capitulary of 56 chapters.

councils.note: The Frankish reaction (Libri Carolini / Opus Caroli regis, by Theodulf of Orléans, c. 790–793) relied on a defective Latin translation of Nicaea II's acts that blurred the distinction between veneration and worship. Spanish Adoptionism (8th c.) differs from 2nd–3rd c. dynamic monarchianism.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Iglesia católica (lo cuenta como el octavo concilio ecuménico). La Iglesia ortodoxa lo rechaza.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church (counted as the eighth ecumenical council). Rejected by the Eastern Orthodox Church.

convokedBy.es: El emperador Basilio I, de acuerdo con el papa Adriano II
convokedBy.en: Emperor Basil I, in agreement with Pope Hadrian II

decisions.es: Del 5 de octubre de 869 al 28 de febrero de 870. Depuso al patriarca Focio y confirmó la restitución de Ignacio. Emitió 27 cánones en la versión latina (menos en la griega), entre ellos el canon 21 sobre el orden de las sedes patriarcales. La asistencia fue escasa al principio (unos 20–25 obispos) y llegó a 102 en la sesión final.
decisions.en: From 5 October 869 to 28 February 870. It deposed Patriarch Photius and confirmed the restoration of Ignatius. It issued 27 canons in the Latin version (fewer in the Greek), including canon 21 on the order of the patriarchal sees. Attendance was small at first (about 20–25 bishops), reaching 102 at the final session.

councils.note: The Latin version has 27 canons; the Greek abridgment has 14. Its acts were annulled by the council of 879–880. When the West began to count it as ecumenical is debated: Francis Dvornik argued it became so only in the late 11th century (Gregorian-reform canonists), after Rome had earlier accepted the 879–880 council.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Algunos teólogos y documentos ortodoxos lo consideran el octavo concilio ecuménico; la Iglesia ortodoxa no lo ha definido formalmente así. La Iglesia católica no lo cuenta como ecuménico.
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Some Orthodox theologians and documents regard it as the eighth ecumenical council; the Orthodox Church has not formally defined it as such. The Catholic Church does not count it as ecumenical.

convokedBy.es: El emperador Basilio I, con legados del papa Juan VIII
convokedBy.en: Emperor Basil I, with legates of Pope John VIII

decisions.es: Con unos 383 obispos y legados papales, reconoció a Focio (restituido tras la muerte de Ignacio en 877) como patriarca legítimo y anuló el concilio de 869–870. Reafirmó el Credo niceno-constantinopolitano prohibiendo añadirle o quitarle nada, lo que la tradición ortodoxa entiende como un rechazo implícito del Filioque.
decisions.en: With about 383 bishops and papal legates, it recognized Photius (restored after Ignatius' death in 877) as legitimate patriarch and annulled the council of 869–870. It reaffirmed the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed and forbade adding to or subtracting from it, which Orthodox tradition reads as an implicit rejection of the Filioque.

councils.note: Whether and how far Pope John VIII approved its acts is contested among historians (Dvornik argued he did; others read his letters as conditional).

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Solo la Iglesia católica (noveno concilio ecuménico en su cómputo).
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church only (ninth ecumenical council in its numbering).

decisions.es: Primer concilio general celebrado en Occidente. Ratificó el Concordato de Worms (1122), que cerró la querella de las investiduras entre el papado y el emperador, y promulgó cánones contra la simonía, el matrimonio y el concubinato del clero y la investidura laica de cargos eclesiásticos.
decisions.en: The first general council held in the West. It ratified the Concordat of Worms (1122), which ended the Investiture Controversy between the papacy and the emperor, and issued canons against simony, clerical marriage and concubinage, and lay investiture of church offices.

councils.note: Canon count varies between collections (22 or 25).

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Solo la Iglesia católica (décimo concilio ecuménico en su cómputo).
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church only (tenth ecumenical council in its numbering).

decisions.es: Cerró el cisma provocado por la elección del antipapa Anacleto II y anuló sus ordenaciones. Emitió 30 cánones; entre ellos declaró que las uniones contraídas por clérigos de órdenes mayores y por religiosos profesos no son matrimonio válido.
decisions.en: It closed the schism caused by the election of the antipope Anacletus II and annulled his ordinations. It issued 30 canons; among them it declared that unions contracted by clergy in major orders and by professed religious are not valid marriages.

recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.es: Solo la Iglesia católica (undécimo concilio ecuménico en su cómputo).
recognizedAsEcumenicalBy.en: Catholic Church only (eleventh ecumenical council in its numbering).
